passage:
My little brother Dhruv came home from school with his shoelace untied and his face all crumpled. I'm Manoj, I'm twelve, and I know that face.
At dinner Papa asked, "How was the week?"
"The worst," Dhruv said. "I lost my pencil box on Monday. Ma'am scolded me on Wednesday. And today nobody picked me for kho-kho."
I reminded him he won the drawing prize on Tuesday. He'd been bouncing about it for hours.
"That doesn't count," he said. "Tomorrow will be bad too. I just know."
I don't know everything going on in his head. Maybe the kho-kho thing hurt more than he's saying. After dinner I asked if he wanted to play carrom. He shrugged, then came.

qa.q: What prize did Dhruv win on Tuesday?
qa.a: The drawing prize.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv say the drawing prize 'doesn't count'?
qa.a: He is upset after not being picked for kho-kho, so right now only the bad things feel real and the good ones seem not to matter.

qa.q: What could Papa or Manoj do the next day to help Dhruv?
qa.a: Once Dhruv is calmer, they could ask him for one good and one bad thing from the day, so the good bits get a chance to be remembered.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Dhruv's 'worst week'?
qa.a: Manoj remembers Dhruv bouncing about the prize, so to Manoj the week looks mixed, and the kho-kho hurt seems to be colouring everything.

grounding: An older sibling watches an upset younger brother list only the week's bad events and predict a bad tomorrow, forgetting a recent prize.

passage:
Monday. Mohit laughed when Divyansh slipped in the corridor, and Divyansh stopped speaking to him. At home he flung his bag down. "This whole week is rubbish. Tomorrow will be rubbish." He couldn't think of one nice thing, not even last Friday's samosa party.
Wednesday. Divyansh sat alone at lunch, sure the maths test would go wrong. It went fine, but he told Nani it was "probably bad."
Saturday. Mohit knocked on the door with a borrowed comic and a sorry. They sat on the steps reading. "Remember the samosa party?" Mohit said, and Divyansh laughed. Suddenly he remembered the sunny PT period and his gold star too. "Huh," he said. "It wasn't all rubbish."

qa.q: What did Mohit bring on Saturday?
qa.a: A borrowed comic and a sorry.

qa.q: Why couldn't Divyansh think of one nice thing on Monday?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry after Mohit laughed, and that sad mood let only bad memories come to mind.

qa.q: What could help Divyansh on a day like Monday?
qa.a: Waiting until he feels calmer, or looking for one good thing from the week, like the samosa party, before deciding the whole week is rubbish.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt hearing the test was 'probably bad'?
qa.a: Nani may have worried, not knowing the test went fine and that his mood was doing the talking.

grounding: Across several days, an upset child sees only bad memories and expects a bad tomorrow, until making up with a friend brings the good ones back.

passage:
Ankita, you've got a face like a rainy day. Let your grandpa tell you something.
When I was ten, in Goa, my best friend moved away to Mumbai. That evening my mother asked how school was. I told her everything was terrible: the teacher hated me, I'd failed my sums, and the monsoon had ruined football. "Tomorrow will be worse," I said.
My mother just said, "Francis, write down the whole week tonight. Good and bad." I sat with the paper, and slowly it came back: nine out of ten in sums. The teacher had let me ring the bell. We'd played football in the rain, laughing.
I was still sad about my friend. But the week wasn't what my sadness said it was.
Now. What happened today?

qa.q: Where did young Francis's best friend move?
qa.a: To Mumbai.

qa.q: Why did ten-year-old Francis think tomorrow would be worse?
qa.a: Sad about losing his friend, he could only recall bad things, so the future looked bad too.

qa.q: Why did his mother's idea help, and could Ankita use it?
qa.a: Writing down the good and the bad brought forgotten good moments back; Ankita could try the same with today.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Ankita might feel understood and less alone, and more ready to tell grandpa about today. 🙂

grounding: A grandfather recalls being a sad ten-year-old who remembered only a bad week and expected worse, until writing it all down showed the good parts.

passage: The rain had flooded the lane outside the school, and Kiran's father was stuck in traffic, so Kiran waited in the empty staff room with Salma aunty, the office helper. Kiran had not won the drawing prize that afternoon. Swinging both legs, Kiran listed everything: "On Monday I spilled milk. On Tuesday I forgot my homework. Today I lost. This whole week was the worst week." "And tomorrow?" Salma aunty asked. "Tomorrow will be bad too. It always is." Salma aunty passed over a biscuit. "Didn't you tell me on Wednesday that your class clapped for your rabbit drawing?" Kiran stopped chewing. "...Oh. Yes." "And yesterday you got to feed the fish." Kiran's legs slowed. Outside, a horn honked twice. "That's Papa!" Kiran grabbed the bag and ran.

qa.q: What did Kiran spill on Monday?
qa.a: Milk.

qa.q: Why did Kiran believe the whole week was the worst?
qa.a: Feeling upset about losing the prize made only the bad moments come to mind, so the good ones, like the rabbit drawing, seemed to disappear.

qa.q: What did Salma aunty do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gently reminded Kiran of good things from the same week, so Kiran could see that sadness had been choosing which memories showed up.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Salma aunty, stuck with an upset child in the rain?
qa.a: Salma aunty stayed patient and kind, sharing a biscuit and listening, even though it meant waiting late at school.

grounding: A child upset after losing a prize remembers only the bad parts of the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage: In their Andheri flat, Deepika, eight, pushed rice around her plate. Her friend had sat with someone else at lunch. "This week was horrible," she told Farida Khala, who had come over for dinner. "On Monday the bus was late. On Tuesday I got a sum wrong. Today nobody sat with me. Tomorrow will be horrible too." Farida Khala raised an eyebrow. "Nothing good at all?" Deepika shook her head firmly, lips tight. Her mother caught Farida Khala's eye and said nothing. Next morning, sunlight on the balcony, Deepika was humming while tying her shoes. "Khala, did I tell you I came first in the sack race on Wednesday?" Farida Khala laughed. "Last night that race didn't exist." Deepika frowned, puzzled. "It was there all along," she said slowly.

qa.q: What did Deepika win on Wednesday?
qa.a: She came first in the sack race.

qa.q: Why couldn't Deepika remember the sack race at dinner?
qa.a: She was hurt about lunch, and the sad mood made her mind pull up only bad moments, so the win did not come to mind at all.

qa.q: How could a grown-up help Deepika the next time she feels sure a whole week was bad?
qa.a: They could wait for a calmer moment, or gently ask about one good thing from each day, so the mood doesn't choose all her memories.

qa.q: How might Farida Khala see the change between dinner and the next morning?
qa.a: Farida Khala seems amused and a little struck by it, seeing how one hurt feeling at night had hidden a happy memory.

grounding: A child upset over lunch remembers only the bad parts of her week and expects tomorrow to be bad, until her mood lifts.

passage: After cricket practice at the Lucknow sports club, Coach Pankaj found Mohit sitting alone on the pavilion steps. Mohit had been bowled out first ball. "How's your week been?" Coach asked. "Bad," Mohit said. "I got a sum wrong on Monday. My bat handle broke. Today I got out. And tomorrow's match will be bad too." Coach sat down. "What about Tuesday's catch? The whole team cheered." Mohit blinked. He had forgotten the catch completely. "And didn't your Nani visit?" "Yes," Mohit said slowly. "She brought laddoos." He still felt sad about getting out. But the week had some good bits hiding in it. Coach handed him a ball. "Ten throws before your papa comes?" Mohit stood up, wiping his nose on his sleeve.

qa.q: What happened to Mohit's bat on his bad week?
qa.a: His bat handle broke.

qa.q: Why did Mohit only remember bad things when Coach asked about his week?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed after being bowled out first ball, and that sadness made the bad moments come to mind first, hiding the catch and his Nani's visit.

qa.q: How could Coach Pankaj help Mohit next time he is upset?
qa.a: He could ask Mohit to name one good thing from the week alongside the hard ones, as he did with the catch and the laddoos.

qa.q: How might Mohit's teammates remember Tuesday differently?
qa.a: They might remember Tuesday as a happy day, since the whole team cheered Mohit's catch.

grounding: Shows a child whose sad mood after a bad game lets only the bad moments of the week come to mind and makes tomorrow seem sure to go badly.

passage:
Monday: Jagdish's new kite tore on the neem tree before it even flew. He sat on the roof and would not come down for dinner.
Tuesday: At school, Yash asked, "How was your weekend?" "Horrible," Jagdish said. "Everything went wrong. And the kite competition on Sunday will be horrible too." Yash looked confused. "But you won at carrom on Saturday. You beat my brother." Jagdish shrugged. It did not feel like it had happened.
Friday: His uncle helped him glue the torn paper, and the kite flew over three rooftops. That evening Jagdish told his mother about the weekend: the carrom win, the jalebis at the fair, Yash's cousin's funny dog. "Wasn't it a horrible weekend?" she teased. Jagdish frowned. "Was it?" Then he laughed and ran back up to the roof.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish's new kite tear?
qa.a: It tore on the neem tree.

qa.q: Why did the carrom win not feel real to Jagdish on Tuesday?
qa.a: He was still upset about his torn kite, and his sad mood only let the bad moments feel real, so the happy win seemed far away.

qa.q: What could Yash do when a friend says everything went wrong?
qa.a: He could gently remind them of one good thing that happened, as he did with the carrom win, and maybe offer to help with the problem.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's mother see his weekend on Friday compared with Tuesday?
qa.a: She hears about the carrom, the jalebis and the funny dog, so she sees a happy weekend and is amused that he once called it horrible.

grounding: Shows a child's sad mood choosing only bad memories and a gloomy forecast, and a better mood later bringing the good memories back.

passage: Lalremsiami, you are sulking about your week? Come, let your Hafsa aunty tell you something. When I was nine, in Aizawl, I cracked my slate on Tuesday and my teacher scolded me in front of everyone. I cried the whole way home. That night I told my father, "This whole week was bad. On Monday I lost my ribbon, on Wednesday it rained, and the fair on Saturday will be bad also." My father did not argue. He asked me, "What did you eat on Thursday?" I said, "Egg curry," and I remembered: my friend Mawii had shared her egg because it was my favourite. Then I remembered I sang in assembly. By the end I was laughing. And the fair was lovely. The week had not changed. Only my sad eyes had.

qa.q: What did young Hafsa crack on Tuesday?
qa.a: She cracked her slate.

qa.q: Why did the whole week seem bad to young Hafsa that night?
qa.a: She was hurt and ashamed after being scolded in front of everyone, so her sadness picked out only the bad moments and made the fair seem sure to be bad too.

qa.q: What choice did Hafsa's father make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He did not argue but asked what she ate on Thursday, which gently led her to remember Mawii's kindness and the singing on her own.

qa.q: How might Mawii have felt about the week if asked?
qa.a: Mawii might remember a happy moment of sharing her egg with a friend, since the egg curry was a kind thing she chose to do.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's childhood memory, how a sad mood made a child recall only bad things and expect the fair to be bad too.

passage:
It was the last day of the school week, and rain had flooded the playground, so there was no games period. Kunal, nine, came home, dropped his bag and flopped on the sofa.

"This whole week was terrible," he told his older cousin Jomon. "I lost my eraser. Everyone laughed at my answer. And tomorrow will be bad too."

Jomon sat beside him. "What about Tuesday? You said you scored full marks in dictation."

Kunal thought. "Oh. Yes."

"And Wednesday you shared lunch with the new boy."

"He liked my aloo paratha," Kunal said, almost smiling.

Jomon ruffled his hair. "Sad days make us remember only sad things. Let's make tea and tell Mausi about the dictation."

qa.q: What did Kunal score in dictation on Tuesday?
qa.a: Full marks.

qa.q: Why did Kunal say the whole week was terrible?
qa.a: He felt sad and fed up after a bad day, and that mood made him remember only the bad things.

qa.q: How did Jomon help Kunal see the week differently?
qa.a: He reminded Kunal of good moments like full marks and sharing lunch, and involved Mausi, a caring adult.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when Kunal almost smiled?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt relieved and glad that his cousin was feeling a little better.

grounding: A child who is upset remembers only bad things about the week and expects tomorrow to be bad, as feelings pick what he recalls.

passage:
Gautam, ten, sat at the dining table in their Kolkata flat, staring at his rice. His best friend had sat with someone else at lunch.

"How was school?" asked his mother Anjali.

"Horrible. Everything this week was horrible. Nobody likes me. And tomorrow's the maths test, and I'll fail it."

Anjali put down her spoon. "Didn't you tell me on Monday you won the class quiz?"

Gautam shrugged. "That doesn't count."

"And yesterday you said the maths practice was easy."

Gautam was quiet. "I forgot."

Anjali held his hand. "When we feel sad, our minds hide the good bits. Let's talk about lunch, and then we'll see how tomorrow feels."

qa.q: What did Gautam win on Monday?
qa.a: The class quiz.

qa.q: Why did Gautam say "Everything this week was horrible"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and sad about lunch, and that feeling made his mind pick only the bad memories and expect more bad things.

qa.q: What did Anjali do that helped Gautam?
qa.a: She gently reminded him of good things from the week, held his hand, and offered to talk about what upset him.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Gautam says "Nobody likes me"?
qa.a: Anjali probably feels worried and sad for her son, and wants to comfort him.

grounding: A child who is upset recalls only bad things from the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage:
"Salma, why are you crying?"

"The whole week was bad, Kishore Bhaiya."

"The whole week?"

"Yes. My drawing got torn. Ma'am scolded me for talking. And I fell in PT."

"What about Tuesday? You showed me the star you got."

"...Oh. Yes."

"And Thursday, didn't you and Ruksar win the relay?"

"We did."

"So not the whole week."

Salma sniffed. "But tomorrow will be bad."

"Why?"

"Because today was."

Kishore sat down next to her. "Let's tell Ammi about the torn drawing. Then tomorrow we'll see."

Salma leaned on his shoulder.

qa.q: Who did Salma win the relay with?
qa.a: Ruksar.

qa.q: Why does Salma think tomorrow will be bad?
qa.a: Salma feels sad and upset about today, so her mind expects more bad things because "today was."

qa.q: What could help Salma when she feels this way again?
qa.a: Remembering good moments, like the star and the relay, and telling a caring adult like Ammi what upset her.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel when Salma leans on his shoulder?
qa.a: Kishore probably feels protective and caring toward his little sister.

grounding: A child who is upset remembers only bad things from the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage: Last winter, on the day my best friend moved away, I sat on the step outside our flat and decided the whole week had been terrible. Maths test: bad. Lost my scarf: bad. Mummy was busy: bad. I told my sister Shalini that tomorrow would be terrible too. She sat next to me and asked, "Eshaan, what about the snowman cake on Tuesday?" I had forgotten it completely. And the kite on Wednesday. And winning at carrom. They were all there, but my sad feeling had hidden them. Now, when I'm sad, I try to remember one good thing from the week. It doesn't fix the sadness, but it makes tomorrow look less scary.

qa.q: What happened on Tuesday that Eshaan had forgotten?
qa.a: The snowman cake.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan decide the whole week had been terrible?
qa.a: Eshaan felt sad because the best friend moved away, and the sadness picked out only the bad memories and hid the good ones.

qa.q: What does Eshaan do now when feeling sad?
qa.a: Tries to remember one good thing from the week, which makes tomorrow look less scary.

qa.q: How does Shalini help, and what might she be feeling?
qa.a: She sits beside Eshaan and asks about the good moments, probably feeling caring and gentle rather than impatient.

grounding: A child who feels sad remembers only the bad parts of the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage: Teacher's note, monsoon term. Nilesh arrived soaked and silent today after his cycle chain broke on the way. At circle time he said, "This week was the worst. Everything went wrong." When I asked for examples, he listed only the broken chain, a low spelling score and losing at kabaddi. Rukmini reminded him that he had won the drawing prize on Monday. He shrugged: "That doesn't count." It seemed to me that his mood was choosing his memories. I sat with him and asked him to name one good thing from each day, and he found three. I will mention the tough week to his parents at pickup.

qa.q: What prize did Nilesh win on Monday?
qa.a: The drawing prize.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh say the drawing prize doesn't count?
qa.a: He was upset and gloomy after the broken chain, so his mood let only bad memories through and made the good one feel unimportant.

qa.q: How did the teacher help?
qa.a: By sitting with him and asking him to name one good thing from each day, so he found three, and by planning to tell his parents at pickup.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini when he shrugs off the prize?
qa.a: Rukmini tries to cheer him up and may feel confused or a little hurt that the reminder doesn't help.

grounding: A child in an upset mood recalls only the bad things from his week.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Summer holidays and everything is rubbish. Zubin didn't invite me to his house. It rained on Monday. My ice cream fell on Wednesday. I got scolded for the broken glass. Tomorrow will be bad too, I just know it.
Later: Mumma read this and asked, "Only bad things, Aadhya?" She made me look at the photos on her phone. On Tuesday I went swimming and did a whole length. On Thursday Nani came to stay. I forgot both!! I was so grumpy my brain only kept the bad bits. Maybe tomorrow won't be bad. Maybe Zubin will call. 🙂

qa.q: What did Aadhya do on Tuesday?
qa.a: Went swimming and did a whole length.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya expect tomorrow to be bad?
qa.a: Aadhya felt grumpy and left out because Zubin didn't invite Aadhya over, and the bad mood kept only bad memories, so the future looked bad too.

qa.q: What helped Aadhya see the week differently?
qa.a: Mumma asking "Only bad things?" and showing photos of the good days, which brought back memories the mood had hidden.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel reading the first part of the diary?
qa.a: Mumma may feel concerned and tender, seeing Aadhya so low, and wants to help Aadhya see the whole week.

grounding: A child in a sad mood remembers only bad things about the week and expects tomorrow to be bad.

passage:
Snow still lay on the roofs of the hill village in the week after Losar, and Hrithik trudged home with his head down. He had dropped his lunch box in the slush.
Dolma Aunty was sweeping her shop steps. "Why the long face?"
"This whole week was bad," Hrithik said. "Monday I lost the race. Tuesday I got a sum wrong. Today the lunch box. And tomorrow will be bad too, I know it."
Dolma Aunty leaned on her broom. "Didn't you win the kite contest on Wednesday? And didn't your teacher put your drawing on the board?"
Hrithik blinked. He had forgotten both. "Oh. Yes."
"Sad days hide the good ones," she said, and handed him a warm momo from the steamer.

qa.q: What did Hrithik drop in the slush?
qa.a: His lunch box.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik think the whole week was bad?
qa.a: He feels sad and upset about the lunch box, so his mind only brings up bad moments and makes tomorrow look bad too.

qa.q: How did Dolma Aunty help Hrithik see the week more fairly?
qa.a: She reminded him of good moments he had forgotten, the kite contest and the drawing on the board, and handed him a warm momo.

qa.q: What might Dolma Aunty notice that Hrithik can't?
qa.a: She can see that his upset mood is picking only the bad memories, since she remembers his good news from the week.

grounding: Shows an upset child who recalls only the bad parts of his week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.
